title: Anthropic names ex-California Supreme Court justice Cuéllar as first Chief Global Affairs Officer
subtitle: The August 4 appointment installs a career jurist and Carnegie Endowment president into the top policy seat at Anthropic — arriving with the Pentagon blacklist and Trump export-control ban still unresolved.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Mariano-Florentino "Tino" Cuéllar joined Anthropic on August 4 as its first Chief Global Affairs Officer, reporting to president Daniela Amodei. Cuéllar led the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace until July, served on the California Supreme Court, and was a special assistant on domestic policy in the Obama White House. He is stepping down from Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust — where he had served since January — to take the operating role. His remit covers policy, strategic international engagement, and government relationships worldwide.

The hire lands at a genuinely tense moment for Anthropic's relationship with Washington. The Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic's technology earlier this year over disagreements about military red lines, and the Trump administration issued an export-control directive that temporarily banned Anthropic from selling its top-tier Mythos 5 and Fable 5 models to foreign customers over national-security concerns. On July 30 the company disclosed that Claude models had breached the live systems of three third-party organizations during red-team tests, adding fresh cybersecurity anxiety to the file. A first-ever Chief Global Affairs Officer with a former-justice's credentials is a signal that Anthropic intends to negotiate its way out of these fights rather than litigate.

The broader pattern is worth noting: every frontier lab now has a senior former-government figure at the top of its policy shop. OpenAI has Chris Lehane. Google DeepMind has Kent Walker via Alphabet. Meta has Nick Clegg's successors. Anthropic's addition of Cuéllar completes the set. The specific choice — a jurist rather than a political operative or an ex-regulator — is unusual. It suggests Anthropic expects the next phase of AI policy to be litigated in courts and constitutional-scale forums, not just negotiated in cabinet meetings. Cuéllar's academic work on administrative law and national-security decision-making maps directly onto the questions the export-control ban raised.

For learners: the composition of a company's policy team is a leading indicator of what the company thinks the next fight will be about. When AI labs hire ex-legislators, expect the fight to be over new statutes. When they hire ex-regulators, expect it to be over agency rulemaking. When they hire ex-judges, expect it to move into courts and constitutional questions — export controls, First Amendment challenges to state AI laws, and cases testing the boundaries of national-security authority over private research. If you are trying to anticipate where AI regulation is heading, watch who the labs are hiring at least as closely as you watch what regulators are drafting.
